title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
hook: a kid tears a page in half, and in half again, and Vaisheshika asks where the tearing has to stop

segments.voice: Yesterday Vaisheshika, the school of Kanada, opened with dharma and with vishesha: each thing is itself. Who did you see as one particular person, instead of a type? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.
screen: `VISHESHA: EACH THING IS ITSELF.` · `NOW, THE ATOMS.`

segments.voice: A kid at the kitchen table has a sheet of paper and a serious expression. She tears it in half. Then she tears one half in half. Then that half. The pieces get smaller, and her fingers get clumsier, until she's pinching a scrap you can barely see. "Can I keep going?" she asks. "Forever?" The grown-up across the table just shrugs. Vaisheshika had an answer. Not forever. Somewhere down there, the tearing has to stop, at something so small it has no halves left to tear. The school gave that something a name, and the name became the idea the school is known for.
screen: `TEARING A PAGE IN HALF.` → `CAN I KEEP GOING FOREVER?` → `NO: THE TEARING STOPS.`

segments.voice: The name is paramanu, often translated atom: the smallest of the small. A paramanu has no parts. Because it has no parts, it can't come apart, so Vaisheshika calls it eternal. It can't be made and it can't be destroyed. You can't see one, either. Why believe in something you can't see? The school's thinkers gave an argument. If you could divide forever, then a mountain would have endless parts, and so would a mustard seed. Endless and endless. And then what makes the mountain bigger? So the dividing must stop somewhere, at a partless thing. That's an inference, the kind of step Nyaya taught us to say out loud. In the classic account the commentators give, atoms join in a ladder. Two atoms pair up. Then pairs gather, and you reach the smallest thing an eye can see: a speck of dust floating in a beam of sunlight. From there, upward, to clay and rivers and mountains. There are atoms of earth, of water, of fire, of air, each kind carrying its own qualities. So here's the shape of the world in this school. Everything you can see is made of parts. Everything made of parts, sooner or later, comes apart: the cup, the house, the body. But what it's made of doesn't vanish. The pieces go back down the ladder and wait. Set beside a cracked cup or a plan that fell through, that's an unusual kind of comfort. Vaisheshika doesn't say nothing is lost. It says the breaking happens in the joints, not in the bottom of things.
screen: `PARAMANU: THE SMALLEST OF THE SMALL.` · `NO PARTS, SO IT NEVER COMES APART.` · `A MOUNTAIN AND A MUSTARD SEED.` · `A SPECK IN A SUNBEAM.` · then, large: `THE BREAKING IS IN THE JOINTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with things made of parts. Settle, and let the breath slow. Notice your body as an assembly: hands, arms, shoulders, the back against the chair, the feet on the floor. Let your attention move from one part to the next. Then think of one thing in your life that has come apart lately, a plan, a routine, maybe something more. Just hold it, without fixing it. Notice that what it was made of, the effort, the care, the time, hasn't simply disappeared. If you pray, you can rest in what you trust does not come apart. The bell holds the time.
Vaisheshika. The school of particulars and of the paramanu: the partless smallest thing, which never comes apart, where all dividing has to stop.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. Today, when something breaks, even something small, remember: the breaking happens in the joints, not at the bottom of things. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Students of Vaisheshika learn the teaching on atoms through the Vaisheshika Sutra and its commentaries, usually alongside Nyaya, as part of traditional Sanskrit study.

fork.setup: you're the kid at the kitchen table, tearing a page in half again and again. can you keep going forever?
options: yes, forever: there's always a smaller half.
no: you reach something partless that can't be torn.
no: the paper just vanishes into nothing.
fork.reveal: Vaisheshika says the dividing stops at the paramanu, a partless thing. otherwise a mountain and a mustard seed would both have endless parts.

original.note: Sanskrit: paramanu, the smallest particle, often translated atom.

trapdoor: what you thought: atoms are a modern idea.
what it means: Vaisheshika reasoned its way to partless, eternal paramanus, so that what breaks comes apart at the joints, not at the bottom.
what a scholar hears: in the classic Vaisheshika account, atoms combine as dyads, then triads, the triad being the smallest visible thing, a mote in a sunbeam.

notes: Editor pass: cut the superlative 'one of its best-known ideas' and the repeated 'ordinary Tuesday' line.
Paramanu glossed 'the smallest of the small' (parama + anu): lexical; confirm.
Atoms as partless and eternal: Vaisheshika Sutra 4.1.1 (sad akaranavan nityam) and following; confirm the sutra reference.
The mountain/mustard-seed argument against infinite divisibility is attributed to 'the school's thinkers'; confirm the source (commentarial; also discussed around Nyaya Sutra 4.2).

Dyad/triad ladder and the mote in a sunbeam (trasarenu) are attributed to 'the classic account the commentators give' (Prashastapada and later); the spoken text gives pairs but no count for the triad; trapdoor floor 3 names dyads and triads. Confirm.
Atoms of earth, water, fire and air: confirm (akasha is not atomic in Vaisheshika).
